Formal backchannel negotiations between Iranian and Western envoys resumed in Muscat on Monday after President Donald Trump suspended strikes on Iran's energy infrastructure over the weekend, even as Tehran publicly denied direct contacts with Washington.

Trump's U-turn reopens Tehran's political faultline. Donald Trump's decision to abandon a planned large-scale military strike against Iran has accelerated regional diplomatic efforts to revive US-Iran negotiations, while deepening political divisions inside Tehran over engagement with Washington.

Aramco sidesteps Hormuz as Iran crisis cuts flows to a tenth. Saudi Aramco is routing crude around the Strait of Hormuz via its East-West pipeline as the Iran-related crisis has cut shipping through the strait to a tenth of pre-conflict levels, Chief Executive Amin Nasser said on Tuesday.

Tehran records heaviest damage in latest war, municipal report shows. Tehran sustained the heaviest damage of any Iranian province during the 40-day conflict with US and Israel, with more than 50,000 homes damaged and the capital accounting for 650 reported strikes, according to a municipal report published on Monday.

US depleted 'virtually all' long-range precision missiles in Iran war - Reuters. The US Army has used "virtually all" of its ATACMS and Precision Strike Missile supplies during the five-month war with Iran, two sources familiar with the data told Reuters.

Tehran hospital nurses beaten, dismissed after labor protest. Nurses at a Tehran hospital were beaten and detained, with scores dismissed or suspended, after staging a strike over poor working conditions, Iran International has learned.

Iran's president met Mojtaba Khamenei in the back seat of a car. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was taken to a secret Tehran location and allowed only minutes in a dark, tinted-window car with a man presented as Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, sources familiar with the episode told Iran International.

Why Afghans still risk death to reach Iran. "Take care of my sons." Those were the final words of Hayatullah, an Afghan migrant who used his phone to record what would become the last moments of his life in the scorching desert as he tried to reach Iran.

Iran eyes Pakistani ports as route around US blockade. Iran is exploring using two of Pakistan’s ports to keep trade moving amid the US blockade of its own ports, a senior Iranian official said on Tuesday.

Anti-Islam posts follow Iran's dawn executions, sparking hardline backlash. Angered by a wave of early-morning executions of protesters and political prisoners, some Iranian social media users have directed their anger at Islam and the morning call to prayer, prompting an IRGC-linked campaign demanding their prosecution.

Iran presses wider Hormuz demands as US says deal may be close. Prospects for reopening the Strait of Hormuz remained uncertain Tuesday as Washington said an agreement could come by Wednesday, while Tehran linked normal shipping to transit fees, sanctions relief, security guarantees and an end to the US naval blockade.

War or government failure? Record inflation fuels political battle in Iran. The latest figures released by the Statistical Center of Iran offer the starkest assessment yet of the country's economy, as record inflation intensifies debate over whether the war or government mismanagement is primarily to blame.

Iran used water hacks to intimidate not cripple, experts say. Cyberattacks targeting water and wastewater facilities in at least seven US states appear to have been intended less to cripple infrastructure than to demonstrate Iranian reach, intimidate the public and shape perceptions, cybersecurity experts told Iran International.

Iran executed at least 56 people since March, UN rights chief says. Iran has executed at least 56 people on national security-related charges since March 19, including 27 in cases linked to protests earlier this year, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Wednesday.

Iran state bank freezes national oil company accounts over debt. An Iranian state-owned bank has frozen accounts belonging to the National Iranian Oil Company over outstanding debt obligations, the IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency reported on Wednesday.

Smokeless tobacco is hooking Iran's schoolchildren. Why is it sold to them?. Schoolchildren in Iran are getting hooked on nas, a cheap smokeless tobacco sold openly within steps of their classrooms, an official warned on Tuesday, as social media users asked why a product this addictive is hawked to children in plain sight.

Iran's parliament fades further from power after the war. Iran's parliament has become all but irrelevant since the war, as power has shifted further toward the Revolutionary Guards and decision-making has moved ever deeper behind closed doors amid the unresolved leadership transition.

New documentary probes Jamshid Sharmahd's abduction and death. Six years after Iranian-German dissident Jamshid Sharmahd vanished during a trip to the United Arab Emirates, many questions surrounding his abduction, imprisonment and death in the custody of the Islamic Republic remain unresolved.

US and Iran seek a new equilibrium neither trusts. A return to the pre-war status quo between Iran and the United States now appears out of reach for both sides, despite their competing claims of victory.

Tehran says any Hormuz accord won't restore pre-war order. Iran and Oman appear close to agreeing new navigation arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz, but Tehran insists any reopening must take place under a new post-war security framework rather than a return to the pre-war status quo.

Au Sénégal, pourquoi Pastef et l’APR se retrouvent unis face à la transhumance politique. Alors qu’approchent les élections locales, les deux partis, pourtant antagonistes, dénoncent de concert la transhumance de certains de leurs élus vers Kiiraay-Les Patriotes républicains, la formation créée en juillet par le président Bassirou Diomaye Faye.

Abdeslam Alaoui Smaili (HPS) : « La part de l’Afrique dans nos revenus va diminuer ». Le spécialiste des solutions de paiement HPS, coté à la Bourse de Casablanca et présent dans 105 pays, veut s’imposer sur les nouveaux outils digitaux. Son PDG détaille sa stratégie de diversification, loin de sa base africaine historique.

Esclaves et révoltés : le premier État né de la révolution des Zanj, ces travailleurs africains du califat. LES GRANDES RÉVOLTES D’ESCLAVES (1/8) – L’État fondé en 869 près de Bagdad par les esclaves révoltés est le premier du genre dans l’histoire de l’humanité. Il n’en existe qu’un seul autre : Haïti.

Football en Côte d’Ivoire : la « short list » de la FIF pour remplacer Emerse Fae. Qui succédera à Emerse Fae sur le banc des Éléphants ? La FIF a prévu de trancher bientôt entre plusieurs prétendants, dont un grand favori. Coulisses.

« Take back Bamenda » : au Cameroun, Joshua Osih et le SDF partent à la reconquête du Nord-Ouest. En perte de vitesse depuis des années dans son historique bastion du Nord-Ouest, le Social Democratic Front (SDF) compte sur les élections locales à venir pour reprendre le flambeau dans cette partie anglophone du pays. Avec une cible en particulier : Bamenda.

Yassir, la super-app algérienne à la stratégie insondable. Près de dix ans après sa création, la start-up algérienne a quelque peu abandonné ses ambitions panafricaines pour exploiter au maximum son potentiel en Algérie. Non sans quelques ratés.

Intérêts gaziers et entraide judiciaire : les raisons pour lesquelles l’Espagne acceptera sans doute d’extrader un opposant algérien. Arrêté à Barcelone, l’homme d’affaires algérien Ayoub Aissiou, proche du clan Bouteflika dans les années 2000, pourrait être renvoyé dans son pays d’origine, où il a été condamné par contumace. Il risque d’être sacrifié sur l’autel de la bonne entente entre Alger et Madrid.

En Guinée, l’opposition appelle « les patriotes » à « mettre fin à la dictature de Mamadi Doumbouya ». Les Forces vives de Guinée (FVG) estiment que « Mamadi Doumbouya et son clan gouvernent par la terreur » et ont déclaré « rejeter » les institutions en place dans le pays. Une colère aussi alimentée par la relaxe, le 27 juillet, du colonel Bienvenu Lamah, un des principaux responsables du massacre du 28 septembre 2009.

Sénégal : 5 questions pour comprendre la stratégie de Bassirou Diomaye Faye face à Ousmane Sonko. En lançant sa propre formation politique Kiiraay-Les Patriotes républicains, le chef de l’État a scellé son divorce avec son ancien allié Ousmane Sonko, dont le parti est majoritaire à l’Assemblée nationale. Une stratégie à quitte ou double pour l’exécutif.

Nigeria : pourquoi TotalEnergies conteste un redressement fiscal de 550 millions de dollars. TotalEnergies attaque le fisc nigérian en justice, contestant des redressements fiscaux qu’elle juge contraires à un accord signé avec la NNPC en 2008. Ce bras de fer s’inscrit dans le contexte de l’ambitieuse réforme fiscale menée par la présidence Tinubu.

Tchad : entre répression et divisions, une opposition qui peine à exister face à Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno. L’opposition tchadienne peine à survivre. Les emprisonnements, les boycotts et les rivalités de leadership ont fait le jeu d’un Mouvement patriotique du salut (MPS) solidement ancré au pouvoir depuis trois décennies.

Quelle stratégie panafricaine pour le marocain Holmarcom ?. Rachat de Crédit du Maroc et de la filiale de BNP Paribas, alliance avec l’IFC… Dix ans après avoir créé Atlanta Assurances Côte d’Ivoire, le groupe de la famille Bensalah ne cache plus ses ambitions d’expansion au sud du Sahara. Mais contrairement à d’autres champions nationaux, sa stratégie africaine est peu lisible.

Sénégal : qui va payer les indemnités dues à Pape Thiaw, sélectionneur limogé ?. Le limogeage de Pape Thiaw après la Coupe du monde a été acté. Mais le paiement des indemnités dues au technicien est suspendu à un accord entre la fédération et son ministère de tutelle, autrement dit l’État.

Esclaves et révoltés : en 1595, à São Tomé, le roi Amador mène les esclaves à la révolte. LES GRANDES RÉVOLTES D’ESCLAVES (2/8) – La petite île occupée par les Portugais pour les besoins de la production sucrière et du commerce des esclaves fut le théâtre d’une révolte aussi importante que méconnue, à la fin du XVIe siècle.

Côte d’Ivoire : le parti de Simone Ehivet Gbagbo accumule les déboires. La récente démission du premier vice-président Dominique Traoré affaiblit un peu plus une formation qui peine à s’implanter après avoir manqué les principaux rendez-vous électoraux et échoué à nouer des alliances susceptibles de lui donner du souffle.

Cameroun : ce qu’il faut retenir des nominations de Paul Biya au sein de l’armée. Absent du pays depuis près de deux mois, le président camerounais a procédé à une série de promotions et nominations au sein de l’armée. L’occasion de verrouiller un peu plus l’appareil militaire, alors que les inquiétudes sur sa santé sont légion.

Côte d’Ivoire, Guinée, RDC… Quand la fièvre des fonds souverains s’empare de l’Afrique. 2025 aura été l’année de tous les records pour la création de fonds souverains sur le continent. Et la tendance se maintient en 2026. Au-delà des effets d’annonce, ces mécanismes qui ont le vent en poupe ont-ils les moyens de leurs ambitions ?

Crise de Ceuta : « Le Maroc a beaucoup changé. Mais à qui profite ce Maroc ? ». L’afflux de migrants marocains à Ceuta n’est pas une répétition de 2021. Khalid Mouna, spécialiste des mobilisations sociales, y voit le symptôme d’inégalités encore trop ignorées, d’un débat politique atone et de profondes tensions au sein de la société marocaine.

Teodorín Obiang contre la France : la bataille pour le contrôle du 42 avenue Foch fait rage. Entre Paris et Malabo, le torchon brûle au sujet de l’avenir de l’ambassade située avenue Foch. Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue, le vice-président équato-guinéen, multiplie les menaces et brandit un joker : l’Africa Corps.

Manuel Moses, l’ingénieur devenu assureur des grands projets africains. Ingénieur civil reconverti dans la finance, Manuel Moses dirige l’Atidi, le plus grand assureur multilatéral de risques politiques d’Afrique. Son ambition : doubler la base de capital de l’institution à 2 milliards de dollars pour débloquer les infrastructures du continent.

« Ni Arabe ni musulman : Algérien et rebelle » – Kateb Yacine raconté par Marcel Péju en 1987. Après quinze années de silence, le grand écrivain faisait son retour dans le monde littéraire. À cette occasion, Marcel Péju, journaliste à Jeune Afrique – après avoir été le secrétaire général de Jean-Paul Sartre à la revue « Les Temps modernes » –, qui le connaissait bien, signait un texte très personnel sur lui.

Achat d’un avion présidentiel au Mali : la Cour suprême confirme la condamnation d’une ex-ministre. La plus haute juridiction malienne a maintenu la peine de dix ans infligée à l’ancienne ministre de l’Économie, Bouaré Fily Sissoko. L’affaire, emblématique des scandales du mandat d’Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta, avait valu au Mali le gel de fonds du FMI.

Vice-président en Centrafrique : entre Sani Yalo et les autres prétendants, Touadéra ne veut pas choisir. Trois ans après l’adoption d’une Constitution qui a créé la fonction de vice-président, Faustin-Archange Touadéra n’a toujours pas désigné celui qui assurerait l’intérim en cas de vacance du pouvoir. Sani Yalo, dont le nom circule, suscite la méfiance de certains. Explications.

Mali : pourquoi Clément Dembélé reste incarcéré, malgré les éléments en sa faveur. La Cour suprême du Mali a rejeté le pourvoi en cassation de Clément Dembélé, militant anticorruption détenu depuis près de trois ans. Une décision contestée par sa défense.

Ceuta : les raisons économiques d’une crise migratoire. Chômage, inégalités, subventions publiques au profit des plus aisés… Au fil des années, au Maroc, une frange de la société, en particulier les jeunes, a vu sa situation économique se détériorer.

Au Sénégal, un lendemain de Magal amer pour les fonctionnaires. Au lendemain du Magal de Touba, pratiquement aucun fonctionnaire sénégalais ne s’est présenté au bureau. En demandant des explications, leur ministre de tutelle a relancé la polémique sur le fait de rendre férié le « jour d’après le jour férié ».

Comment le Gabon veut remettre son projet avec Suez sur les rails. Le poids lourd français de la gestion de l’eau et des déchets doit aider Libreville à redresser le segment des services hydriques. Mais ce partenariat peine encore à décoller. Explications.

Entre Centrafrique et Soudan, reportage à Birao, ville aux portes de la guerre. En visite dans la Vakaga quelques semaines après les attaques d’Amdafock, Félix Moloua, le Premier ministre centrafricain, a voulu montrer que l’État tenait bon. Mais la population redoute une nouvelle attaque, dans un climat de crise larvée.

Cameroun : l’absence prolongée de Paul Biya embarrasse les milieux diplomatiques. Parti le 7 juin pour un « court séjour privé en Europe », Paul Biya n’est toujours pas rentré au Cameroun. Son absence prolongée inquiète les partenaires étrangers, qui peinent à identifier les véritables centres de décision au sommet de l’État. Coulisses.

Au Maroc et au Gabon, des fonds souverains aux trajectoires mouvementées. Dix ans après sa transformation, le marocain Ithmar Capital se cherche toujours une vocation tandis que son homologue gabonais, le FGIS, tente de tourner définitivement la page des années Bongo.

Crise de Ceuta : Giorgia Meloni, bénéficiaire de la solidarité de Bruxelles, en 2023, à Lampedusa, veut isoler l’Espagne. La présidente d’extrême droite du conseil italien veut se positionner comme une leader en Europe sur le thème migratoire, à l’approche d’une campagne électorale qui s’annonce dominée par les discours identitaires.

Au Nigeria, au moins 52 personnes kidnappées par des hommes armés dans le nord-ouest du pays. Des hommes armés ont fait irruption à moto, pendant la nuit de samedi à dimanche, dans le village de Kasuwar Daji, dans la zone de gouvernement local de Kaura Namoda, où ils ont d’abord attaqué une base militaire située à la périphérie de la localité.

« Mettre le feu, c’est le moyen le plus rapide d’être renvoyé chez soi » : au Kenya, le système des internats au bord de l’implosion. Au début du mois de juin, le ministère de l’éducation kényan recensait 204 établissements touchés par des dégradations de la part d’élèves scolarisés. Ces derniers déplorent des conditions de vie trop strictes, des infrastructures vétustes et des punitions physiques. Fin mai, 16 pensionnaires sont morts dans l’incendie de leur dortoir.

Au Mali, l’ancien premier ministre Moussa Mara est sorti de prison. Chef du gouvernement malien pendant huit mois, en 2014-2015, l’opposant avait été arrêté en août 2025 après avoir rendu visite à des prisonniers politiques.

Catherine Wihtol de Wenden, politiste : « Le Maroc a pris conscience depuis longtemps de la place géostratégique qu’il occupe pour l’Europe en termes de migrations ». Comme tend à le montrer l’afflux de migrants dans l’enclave de Ceuta, les 30 et 31 juillet, le royaume chérifien semble utiliser la question migratoire dans sa stratégie diplomatique, à l’image de la Turquie ou de la Biélorussie, analyse la spécialiste des migrations internationales dans une tribune au « Monde ».

Au Sénégal, les grandes figures de l’islam soufi inspirent les discours souverainistes et anticolonialistes. Les références à Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba, fondateur de la confrérie des mourides, ou El Hadj Oumar Tall, leader de la tidjaniya, continuent d’irriguer les champs politiques sénégalais.

Au Soudan, les défections se multiplient dans les rangs des paramilitaires, au profit de l’armée. Depuis le mois d’avril, des dizaines de combattants des Forces de soutien rapide de « Hemetti » ont rejoint les Forces armées soudanaises du général Al-Bourhane. Des ralliements qui fragilisent les paramilitaires, mais qui ne sont pas sans risque pour Khartoum.

Crise de Ceuta : l’impossible quête des origines de la rumeur d’une ouverture de la frontière. Les messages et vidéos publiés sur Facebook, TikTok ou Instagram semblent avoir largement contribué à l’afflux de candidats à l’exil à Ceuta, fin juillet. A ce stade, rien ne prouve qu’il ait pu s’agir d’une opération de déstabilisation.

Hervé Renard nouveau sélectionneur de la Côte d’Ivoire, onze ans après son sacre en Coupe d’Afrique des nations avec les Eléphants. Le Français, nommé mardi, remplace Emerse Faé et retrouve une équipe avec qui il a déjà remporté la CAN en 2015.

Ceuta : au moins 77 personnes sont mortes en voulant rejoindre l’enclave espagnole, selon les autorités locales. Selon l’Association marocaine des droits humains, le bilan atteint « près de 130 victimes » avec « des dizaines de disparus ».

Crise de Ceuta : le Maroc appelle l’Union européenne à ne pas « handicaper » son développement. Le ministère de l’intérieur marocain et celui des affaires étrangères ont pris la parole, dimanche et lundi, rejetant la responsabilité de la crise migratoire sur le gouvernement de Pedro Sanchez.

Crise de Ceuta : « Le Maroc n’a pas besoin d’un nouveau plan de développement, mais d’un nouveau contrat social ». Fin juillet, près de 50 000 migrants venus du Maroc sont entrés dans l’enclave espagnole. Plutôt qu’une crise migratoire, il faut y voir l’échec du pacte de croissance mis en place par les élites marocaines, analyse l’économiste Jamal Bouoiyour dans une tribune au « Monde ».

La guerre en Somalie, l’autre impasse stratégique de l’administration Trump. L’armée américaine intervient dans ce pays de la Corne de l’Afrique depuis plus de vingt ans. Avec le retour de Donald Trump à la Maison Blanche, le nombre de frappes a quadruplé par rapport au bilan des quatre années de mandat de Joe Biden.

« Cotton Queen » : au Soudan, le cri de résistance de deux générations de femmes. Le film, qui mêle accents poétiques et réalités documentaires, voit la propriétaire d’un champ de coton et sa petite-fille confrontées à l’arrivée d’un homme d’affaires puissant.

« Ma tête a été mise à prix par le fils du président » : Bobi Wine, le premier opposant en Ouganda, raconte sa fuite du pays. Alors que les autorités ougandaises s’apprêtaient à l’arrêter, le chanteur de raggamuffin a trouvé refuge à Washington, en mars. Pour « Le Monde », il revient sur sa cavale de deux mois et sur l’état de l’opposition dans le pays d’Afrique de l’Est.

« La France aime les gens gentils » : une vidéo embarrassante de l’ambassade française au Congo refait surface. « Le Canard enchaîné » a exhumé, mardi 4 août, un clip vidéo produit par l’ambassade de France à Brazzaville, publié en juin et supprimé au bout de quelques heures. Centrée sur l’épineuse question des visas, la vidéo est jugée raciste par de nombreux internautes.

« Gianni Infantino doit avoir le courage de démissionner ou de solliciter un vote de confiance », estime le Congolais Constant Omari, ancien membre du conseil de la FIFA. L’ex-président par intérim de la Confédération africaine de football estime, dans un entretien au « Monde », que les dirigeants africains du football « doivent ouvrir les yeux et les bons » sur le président de la FIFA, fragilisé depuis l’abandon de son projet de création de société commerciale.
Au Nigeria, plus de 300 victimes d’enlèvements ont été libérées. Les victimes ont été libérées d’un lieu situé dans la forêt du parc national du lac Kainji.

Ceuta : pourquoi la crise migratoire interroge sur les relations diplomatiques entre le Maroc et l’Espagne ? Comprendre en trois minutes. L’arrivée d’environ 70 000 personnes en provenance du Maroc dans l’enclave espagnole, les 30 et 31 juillet, s’inscrit dans une longue histoire de tensions entre Madrid et Rabat.

Dans l’est de la RDC, où sévit l’épidémie d’Ebola, la baisse des aides internationales fragilise la prise en charge des plus démunis. Les Etats-Unis étaient le premier bailleur bilatéral du pays en matière d’aide au développement et le premier contributeur au financement du plan de réponse humanitaire.

Trump, Netanyahu clash over Iran strategy and Lebanon ceasefire. DUBAI: American President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have found themselves at odds over Iran, Lebanon and the course of ongoing negotiations in the Middle East according to The Washington Post.

Trump warns Iran to open Strait of Hormuz or get 'hit very hard'. United States President Donald Trump said a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could come as soon as Wednesday but warned Iran it would get “hit very hard” if negotiations fell through. Transit of the waterway, a key conduit for global oil and gas supplies, has been a sticking point in talks and led to renewed fighting following an April ceasefire . Iran has tightened its grip on Hormuz and wants to control the strait and charge tolls — powers it did not exercise before the war began on February 28. Trump said on Tuesday a deal with Iran to reopen Hormuz could happen “tomorrow or the next day,” telling reporters in California that negotiators “had a very good day”. Earlier, he struck a more threatening tone. “The strait is going to be open very soon, or they’re going to get hit very hard — and then the strait’s going to be open,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News. “All you can do is fight your way out.” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC earlier “there is a chance we may have a deal” by Wednesday or Thursday. Underlining the volatile situation, one crew member was listed missing Tuesday on a merchant ship hit by a projectile in Hormuz, while an Indian ship in the Red Sea sank following an unattributed attack. In what has become a regular pattern, Trump last week threatened to hit Iran “very hard”, potentially with attacks against civilian infrastructure, only to pull back, hinting a deal was near. Iran’s foreign ministry has denied negotiations with Washington, even as Trump insisted they were happening. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that the US was involved in negotiations between Oman and Iran on increasing traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. News outlet Axios reported on Tuesday that the US, Iran and Oman were nearing an interim deal to reopen the strait, which Washington was hoping to announce on Wednesday. Axios , citing unnamed regional officials and a US official, said the deal on the table would be a 60-day arrangement for safe passage in the strait between Iran and Oman. Deal or surrender Qatar, which has been mediating negotiations, said that diplomatic efforts were ongoing but that no direct Iran-US talks were planned. Its leader, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani, spoke with Trump by phone on Tuesday, with Doha saying they discussed “efforts to de-escalate tensions.” Trump had previously said he expected to know by Tuesday how the talks were going, “one way or the other”, but insisted “it’s not very complex”. Washington’s diplomatic goals include reopening Hormuz and the denuclearisation of Iran, which Trump accepted could “take a little while.” The president previously called Tehran “ duplicitous ” for saying it was not negotiating, adding that a US counter-blockade of Iranian ports would remain “unless a Deal, or Total Surrender, is accomplished”. More than five months into a war that has cost Washington billions of dollars, Iran remains able to fire missiles and drones at US and allied targets in the region, as well as at commercial shipping. Early on Tuesday, Britain’s maritime security agency UKMTO said an unnamed cargo vessel had been struck by an “unknown projectile” in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman. Iran continues to impose an effective blockade on the strait and insists ships coordinate crossings with it. Red Sea attack The disruptions in Hormuz have only placed greater importance on shipping lanes through the Red Sea, where Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu has enabled it to keep up shipments to global markets by circumventing Hormuz entirely. But since the Houthis announced their blockade, they have claimed attacks on multiple ships they say are in violation. On Tuesday, the Indian ship MSV Faize Noore Oliya sank in the Red Sea off Yemen following an unattributed attack, with all of its crew rescued. The Red Sea is a gateway to the Suez Canal, and a previous campaign of Houthi attacks on commercial vessels during the Gaza war forced shippers to instead take lengthy detours around the southern tip of Africa.

Piece of SpaceX rocket believed to have crashed into the moon. A SpaceX rocket piece floating in space since last year was expected to have smashed into the moon at high speed early on Wednesday morning, though the impact was unlikely to be confirmed for at least several hours. The school-bus-size object is the second stage of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket that had launched a lunar lander from Firefly Aerospace toward the moon in January 2025. Weighing four metric tons, the rocket body had been due to hit the moon around 2:35am ET (11:35am PKT), travelling at 5,400 miles per hour, but none of the spacecraft orbiting the moon were expected to be in a position to capture images of the impact live. The space junk would have kicked up a plume of lunar dust that would likely be illuminated by sunlight but difficult to spot with the naked eye from Earth. It was likely to be at least several hours before scientists would be able to confirm the crash by studying images from telescopes in the Americas, the BBC reported. The impact was unintentional, SpaceX said. The rocket piece was expected to hit Einstein Crater on the moon’s western limb, which is often difficult to see from Earth. Cosmic forces nudged piece to moon Such stages typically fall back into Earth’s atmosphere and burn up or plunge into the ocean after boosting the rocket’s payload to a precise spot in orbit. But because the January lunar lander mission required more thrust than missions closer to Earth, the rocket’s second stage remained in space, floating aimlessly among thousands of other pieces of space junk that active satellites must steer clear of. It was not until earlier this year that astronomers determined that the rocket stage, which had dumped its remaining fuel and could not be controlled, was on an orbital trajectory ending at the moon. “What has happened is essentially a mixture of solar activity and gravity forces has put it on a path toward the moon,” Julianna Scheiman, SpaceX director of Nasa science and Dragon programmes, told reporters on Monday. “This may be of some probably minor scientific interest, and we may learn some things from it,” said Bill Gray, creator of widely used astronomy software who published a report on the stage’s impact in April. “It doesn’t present any danger to anyone, though it does highlight a certain carelessness about how leftover space hardware (space junk) is disposed of.” Space junk impacts on the moon are rare. A Chinese rocket stage crashed into the moon in March 2022 after completing a lunar test mission. In 2009, Nasa intentionally crashed a rocket stage into the moon to study the plume of lunar material kicked up by the impact. Several spacecraft intending to softly land on the moon in recent years have crashed instead. Russia’s nuclear-powered Luna-25 mission spun out of control and crashed in 2023. Its small power source of plutonium-238 likely remains harmlessly on the lunar surface. India’s Chandrayaan-2 lander mission crashed in 2019. Israel’s Beresheet lander crashed that same year. Among the Israeli lander’s payloads were tiny tardigrades, microscopic animals known for surviving radiation and other harsh environments and which may still be on the surface. Nasa intentionally crashed stages from its Saturn V moon rocket into the moon in the 1970s to study the impacts’ seismic effects. Nasa and SpaceX are discussing ways to prevent future lunar impacts, Scheiman said. The US space agency plans to build a lunar base and send routine astronaut missions to the lunar surface beginning later this decade under its multibillion-dollar Artemis programme . It would not want errant pieces of space junk impacting those assets.

AJK elections: PML-N, PPP secure one seat each following delayed polls in Muzaffarabad constituencies. MUZAFFARABAD: The PML-N and PPP have secured one seat each in the two constituencies of Muzaffarabad division where polling was held on Tuesday after being fully or partially deferred due to landslides and adverse weather that blocked roads and prevented the timely dispatch of polling staff and election material. The contest was part of the second phase of elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), during which candidates vied for seats in Muzaffarabad division and 12 seats reserved for refugees from India-occupied Kashmir. According to official results released by the AJK Election Commission, PML-N’s Noreen Arif bagged the LA-27 (Kutla) seat with 18,919 votes, beating first runner-up, Sardar Tabarak Ali of the Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party (IPP) by 298 votes. PPP’s Sardar Javed Ayoub was the second runner-up, with 18,037 votes. Meanwhile, PPP’s Syed Bazil Ali Naqvi bagged 28,214 votes to win the LA-28 (Lachhrat) seat, where PML-N’s Chaudhry Shahzad Mahmood secured 26,866 votes to emerge as the first runner-up. The third runner-up, Syed Yasir Hussain Naqvi of All Jammu and Kashmir Conference, managed to get just 873 votes. Along with these results, the Election Commission also notified the returned candidates for the rest of the seats that were up for grabs in the second phase of the elections. The total number of seats won by the PML-N stands at 24 while the PPP has bagged 10. The PML-N had secured nine of the 13 seats in the first phase of the elections in Mirpur division while the PPP had secured four. After Sunday’s and Tuesday’s elections in the second phase, the PML-N bagged 15 more seats, while the PPP managed to add just six more to its tally. The third and final phase of the elections will be held in AJK’s Poonch division on August 10, during which 11 seats will be up for grabs. Elections in AJK are being held in three phases over security concerns and amid protests by the now proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee. Since early June, AJK has witnessed protests by the JAAC, which has been demanding the abolition of the 12 refugee seats in the AJK legislature. The protests have also been marred by violence . Meanwhile, scuffles, violence and allegations of rigging had marred the polls, with the PML-N and PPP accusing each other of electoral malpractices.

Pakistan, US hold counter-terrorism dialogue, reaffirm commitment to combating terrorist groups. WASHINGTON: The United States and Pakistan on Tuesday held the fourth counter-terrorism dialogue in Washington, reaffirming their commitment to combating terrorist groups and strengthening security cooperation at a time when regional tensions remain high. The talks were led by US Coordinator for Counterterrorism Ambassador Gregory LoGerfo and Foreign Ministry Special Secretary Ambassador Nabeel Munir, a joint statement released by the US State Department said. “The dialogue underscored shared interests in the US-Pakistan counter-terrorism partnership and the two countries’ determination to confront terrorism,” the joint statement said. “Delegations exchanged views on the current threat environment, explored avenues to enhance collaboration, and discussed steps to strengthen border security and disrupt terrorist facilitation networks,” it added. The statement specifically named ISIS-Khorasan (ISIS-K), Al Qaeda, the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), and the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) and its affiliates among organisations that both governments said posed threats to regional security. “The US and Pakistan affirmed their joint resolve to confront terrorist organisations that endanger the safety of their citizens and the stability of the region,” the statement said. “The two governments committed to ensuring their counter-terrorism collaboration to keep both of their nations safe and secure, and as part of an enduring vision of regional peace, prosperity, and stability,” it said. Meanwhile, the Foreign Office said that the two sides held “extensive deliberations on the regional and global terrorist threat and pledged to deepen counter-terrorism collaboration both bilaterally and at multilateral fora”. The renewed engagement marks a shift from the difficult period in US-Pakistan relations following the withdrawal of American forces from Afghanistan in 2021. Washington had expressed concerns over terrorists sanctuaries in the region, while Islamabad repeatedly highlighted the security challenges it faced from cross-border militancy and instability in Afghanistan. In recent years, both countries have sought to focus on areas of mutual interest, including counter-terrorism, trade, investment, climate cooperation, and regional stability. Pakistan’s strategic location and longstanding diplomatic links with neighbouring countries have also increased its importance in regional diplomacy. The country’s diplomatic role also gained renewed attention during the US-Iran conflict, as Islamabad has mediated between the two sides. The improved engagement with the US also comes as Pakistan continues to face serious internal security challenges . According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies , an Islamabad-based think tank, violence linked to terrorist attacks and counter-terrorism operations intensified sharply in July, making it the deadliest month of 2026, with 112 security personnel among 205 people killed. Pakistan, US look to finalise reciprocal trade framework While representatives from the US and Pakistan held counter-terrorism discussions in Washington, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb held a virtual meeting with United States Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer from Islamabad. The meeting was held to review the progress of ongoing negotiations, which are focused on strengthening bilateral trade and economic cooperation between Pakistan and the US, a statement released by the finance ministry said. The engagement took place roughly three weeks after the finance minister visited Washington , where he held talks with senior American officials on trade, tariffs, investment and economic cooperation. During his visit, Aurangzeb held meetings with officials from the Office of the Trade Representative, the US Export-Import Bank (Exim), the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and the International Monetary Fund. The discussions focused on a possible bilateral trade agreement covering tariffs, market access, investment opportunities and wider economic cooperation. Separate talks with the Exim Bank and the DFC explored financing for infrastructure, energy and private-sector investment projects in Pakistan. During the meeting on Wednesday, he recalled his recent discussions in Washington and “welcomed the steady progress made by the respective negotiating teams and appreciated the constructive engagement that has characterised the dialogue over time”, the finance ministry said. It added that both sides noted that negotiations on the proposed reciprocal trade framework had advanced significantly and reaffirmed their shared commitment to conclude the agreement at the earliest. “The finance minister highlighted the importance of maintaining the momentum of negotiations in view of Pakistan’s economic priorities. “He emphasised that a strengthened trade and investment partnership with the United States would contribute to Pakistan’s export-led growth strategy, support economic resilience, and create greater commercial opportunities for businesses in both countries,” the statement read. It further said that Aurangzeb also underlined the importance of continued collaboration with the Exim Bank to facilitate bilateral trade and investment. According to the finance ministry, Ambassador Greer acknowledged Pakistan’s continued engagement throughout the negotiations. He reaffirmed the United States’ commitment to “sustaining the positive trajectory of bilateral trade discussions and expressed confidence that the remaining issues could be resolved through continued technical engagement”, the finance ministry said. It added that Aurangzeb also emphasised the importance of maintaining close coordination and accelerating technical-level discussions to build on the progress already achieved. “Both sides expressed satisfaction with the progress achieved and agreed to continue working closely to finalise the remaining elements of the framework and agreed to continue regular engagement with a view to concluding the reciprocal trade framework soon, further strengthening the longstanding economic partnership between Pakistan and the United States,” the ministry’s statement read. It added that Greer also “appreciated the progress made on labour and regulatory reforms, including measures relating to forced labour compliance”. Pakistan is among the 60 countries on which the US imposed new import tariffs last month over what Washington said was their failure to effectively prohibit imports of goods produced with forced labour. Pakistan was placed in the lower 10 per cent tariff category, alongside countries that had either adopted forced labour import prohibitions, committed to doing so under reciprocal trade arrangements, or had partial enforcement regimes. The finance ministry said that Pakistan’s Federal Secretary for Commerce Jawad Paul and senior team members of the USTR also joined Wednesday’s meeting.

Michigan primary puts Democratic divide on the ballot. US Democrats are awaiting results from their marquee primary in Michigan on Wednesday morning, with the contest between a left-wing insurgent and an establishment-backed congresswoman becoming a proxy war over Israel, electability, and the future of the national party. Hours after polls closed, leftist Abdul El-Sayed held a narrow lead over centrist Haley Stevens, with the race too close to call. With 95 per cent of votes counted, NBC was the only major US media outlet to call the race as of 6:50am (3:50pm PKT), projecting a win for El-Sayed. The winner will face former Republican congressman Mike Rogers in November for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, a race central to the party’s difficult effort to win control of the Senate. Democrats must defend Michigan while gaining four Republican-held seats to control the upper chamber, making the primary more than an ideological exercise in a state that has swung between the two parties in recent national elections. Analysts say the results will show whether a current leftist surge among Democrats can move beyond safe seats and win in battlegrounds with national consequences — or whether Michigan’s Democratic establishment can still hold the line. El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director backed by leftist leaders Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, has cast himself as a working-class fighter willing to confront corporations, party leaders and increasingly unpopular pro-Israel donors. Stevens, a four-term lawmaker from the Detroit suburbs, has built her campaign around experience, manufacturing and electability. She is supported by establishment figures from Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer to Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer. ‘Off the hook’ Several recent polls have shown El-Sayed ahead, raising the prospect of the left’s biggest victory yet in a primary season marked by a series of anti-establishment wins. His allies say the campaign’s volunteer energy proves progressives can build a statewide coalition without relying on Washington’s traditional donor network. Stevens is counting on support that she says may be under-represented in opinion polls — from Black voters, older Democrats and people without college degrees. “We’re still getting a ton of votes. We’re firing people up,” she told reporters after casting her ballot in Birmingham, a half-hour drive northwest of Detroit. “My phone’s been ringing off the hook with people who are excited to go to the polls, to see a campaign like mine go forward for November.” The bitterest divide has been over the United States’ deep support for Israel. Stevens has defended continued military backing for the country and rejected accusations that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. El-Sayed has called for an end to unconditional US aid, attacked the influence of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) lobby group, and said Israel should not exist specifically as a Jewish state. ‘Brutality’ AIPAC spending and outside advertising totaling $90 million — in a state with a large Arab-American population and deep anger over the Gaza conflict — has made Michigan another national test of the pro-Israel lobby’s ability to shape Democratic primaries. The candidates have traded increasingly personal attacks, with El-Sayed calling Stevens “the least capable candidate in America”, while she has accused him of blaming his problems on Jewish Americans. Congresswoman Debbie Dingell, who has remained neutral, warned that the “brutality” and “ugliness” of the campaign could make it harder for Democrats to unite afterwards. Michigan voted narrowly for President Donald Trump in 2024, even as Democrat Elissa Slotkin edged Rogers in that year’s Senate race, underscoring both the state’s competitiveness and the risks of a divided party. “The Democratic establishment threw everything it had at Abdul El-Sayed. If he wins, the reverberations will be felt far outside of Michigan,” Dan Pfeiffer, a senior aide in Barack Obama’s White House turned political analyst and podcast host, posted on X. “This would be the second time this cycle that a Schumer-backed candidate was rejected by the voters, which will raise even more questions about whether he and his operation have lost touch with the Democratic base.”

Strong El Nino could push 49 million more people into acute hunger, UN agency says. A powerful El Nino weather event could push an additional nearly 49 million people into acute food insecurity across some of the world’s most vulnerable regions by the end of next year, the World Food Programme (WFP) said on Wednesday. The UN agency said in a report that there was an 81 per cent chance of a very strong El Nino event, with sea surface temperatures at their warmest levels since at least 1982 and potentially making it the strongest such event since 1950. El Nino, a periodic warming of ocean surface temperatures in the Pacific, alters global weather patterns and is often associated with drought in Southern Africa, delayed monsoons in parts of Asia and erratic rainfall elsewhere. “These are events that in the past have triggered large-scale hunger,” Jean-Martin Bauer, director of WFP’s Food Security and Nutrition Analysis Service, told reporters. Based on an analysis of 45 countries deemed vulnerable to the adverse effects of El Nino, WFP estimates that the number of people facing acute food insecurity could rise by almost 49 million to a total of 274 million people, an increase of 22pc, relative to the baseline population already experiencing crisis-level food insecurity or worse. Central America and Southern Africa are expected to be among the hardest-hit regions, with the number of food-insecure people set to increase by 83pc in Central America and nearly 75pc in Southern Africa, the WFP report said. Southern Africa as well as South America and the Caribbean could each see more than 12 million additional people fall into acute food insecurity. Bauer said global food markets entered the El Nino period in a relatively strong position following good harvests in 2025, but warned that conflict in the Middle East and potential weather-related crop losses could put further upward pressure on prices. While past El Nino events have not typically triggered major global food price spikes, regional shortages and higher prices could worsen food access for vulnerable households, he said. Funding cuts from US and European donors in 2025 were also hampering efforts to monitor the developing crisis, with Bauer describing a growing drought of food-security data used to assess the impact of El Nino. WFP conducted about 1.1 million household surveys in 2024, compared with about 800,000 in 2025, while data collection has fallen further this year due to funding restrictions. “At a time when you have a risk like an El Nino, it is important to have high-frequency data collection,” Bauer said, warning that reduced monitoring could make it harder to identify emerging food crises quickly. Early action required WFP said current forecasts point to rainfall deficits in parts of East Africa, the Sahel, Central America and the Caribbean, while flood risks could rise in Somalia and neighbouring areas. Significant impacts are also projected across South and Southeast Asia, where drought risks, uneven monsoons and localised flooding could disrupt agricultural production, the report stated. The agency stressed that the forecasts remain uncertain and that impacts will vary across regions, but warned that governments and aid agencies needed to prepare. Richard Choularton, director of WFP’s Climate and Resilience Service, said the agency had scaled up anticipatory action programmes in 18 countries, reaching more than 1.3 million people so far this year with cash and other assistance to help in the event of extreme weather.

Search team reaches Broad Peak base camp with body of renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja. A search team has transported the bodies of renowned climber Nirmal Purja and three of his team members to the base camp of the mountain where they were killed in an avalanche, the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) said on Wednesday. The avalanche struck on July 30, cutting off contact with the 10-member international expedition led by 43-year-old British-Nepali climber Purja on Broad Peak, one of the world’s highest mountains. His company confirmed there were no survivors . “On behalf of the Alpine Club of Pakistan, it is announced with great sadness to confirm that, following an exceptionally challenging and technically demanding recovery operation on Broad Peak, the bodies of Nirmal Purja, Zhong Wang, Nima Sherpa, and Kilu Sherpa have been successfully recovered and have now arrived safely at Base Camp,” the ACP posted on social media, referring to a Chinese mountaineer and two other Nepali climbers. “While today marks an important milestone, three climbers remain missing,” the club said. “We remain committed to supporting all possible efforts to locate and recover them, whenever conditions allow, so that they too may be returned home to their loved ones,” it added. The remains of three other members of the team — an American woman, an Omani woman and a Nepali man — had already been flown off the mountain to Skardu. The bodies of Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi of Hunza and two Nepali nationals have not yet been recovered. Funeral prayers were offered in absentia for Sakhi in his hometown of Aliabad in Hunza on Monday, where hundreds of people paid tribute to the young mountaineer and offered condolences to his family. Shock and grief have hit members of the alpine climbing community with the President of Nepal’s National Mountain Guide Association Tul Singh Gurung saying they had “lost a generation of accomplished mountaineers”. The ACP said the recovered bodies of the four climbers would be returned to their families. The club’s president, Major General (retd.) Irfan Arshad Khan, told Dawn that the deceased climbers would be airlifted to Skardu by helicopters, which had been unable to operate for the last three days due to adverse weather conditions. “We hope this recovery brings them a measure of peace and the opportunity to lay their loved ones to rest with the dignity they deserve,” the club said. It extended its gratitude to those leading and supporting rescue efforts — including the ground recovery team led by Mingma G and supported by Sirbaz Khan — as well as the dedicated Pakistani and Nepali recovery teams, the Pakistan Army, the governments of Pakistan and Gilgit-Baltistan, local authorities, the British High Commission, and the Embassy of Nepal for their invaluable support throughout the mission. Nirmal’s business partner and Member of Nepal’s House of Representatives Mingma David Sherpa, who is currently monitoring the rescue and search operation, appreciated the “courage, professionalism, and selfless commitment” of the ground recovery team, saying, “We are deeply grateful to every member of the team for carrying out this mission under extremely difficult and dangerous conditions.” “Our thoughts also remain with the families of the three climbers who are still missing. We remain committed to supporting every possible effort to bring them home when conditions safely allow,” he added. Broad Peak is the world’s 12th highest mountain, located in the Karakoram range, and is regarded as one of the toughest and most technical climbs of all the 8,000-metre-plus ascents. It was first summited in 1957 by an Austrian team.

PM Shehbaz directs adoption of comprehensive strategy to attract investors for Discos' privatisation. ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday directed relevant authorities to adopt a “comprehensive strategy” to attract international investors for the privatisation of state-owned power distribution companies (Discos) and complete the restructuring of the Privatisation Commission within one month. “A comprehensive and effective strategy should be adopted to ensure the participation of investors meeting international standards in the privatisation of Discos,” the PM said while presiding over a review meeting in Islamabad, according to a statement issued by his office. But, consumers’ interests should also be prioritised in the privatisation process, he instructed. The premier further stated that all stages of the privatisation process should be completed within the stipulated timeframes and in accordance with established rules and international best practices while ensuring profitable outcomes. He also expressed satisfaction over “successful roadshows” in Pakistan and abroad to attract investors, noting that the shows generated interest in the privatisation programme. Officials at the meeting told the PM that the roadshows aimed at attracting investors for the Gujranwala Electric Power Company (Gepco), Faisalabad Electric Supply Company (Fesco) and Islamabad Electric Supply Company (Iesco) in the first phase of privatisation had been concluded, according to the PMO. It added that the meeting was told that investor outreach activities and roadshows in Turkey, Saudi Arabia and China had produced encouraging results. The meeting was also briefed on the progress of the first phase of Discos’ privatisation and efforts to strengthen the Privatisation Commission through institutional restructuring and the recruitment of skilled professionals. Regarding this, the PM directed that the Privatisation Commission should strengthen its workforce by recruiting experts with qualifications meeting international standards in the fields of finance, law and information technology. Their expertise would enhance the institution’s capacity and help attract greater investment, he remarked. PM Shehbaz also directed relevant officials to ensure that recommendations from highly qualified professional consultants were incorporated in the privatisation process and all necessary legal arrangements and financial regulatory frameworks were completed in a timely manner. Moreover, “consumers’ interests must remain a priority during privatisation and a comprehensive and effective grievance redress mechanism be formed for the consumers of entities being privatised”, he said. Energy Minister Sardar Awais Ahmed Khan Leghari, Economic Affairs Minister Ahad Khan Cheema, Information Technology Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja, PM’s Adviser on Privatisation Muhammad Ali and senior government officials attended the meeting, the PMO stated. On May 19, the Privatisation Commission had invited expressions of interest from local and international investors for the much-delayed sale of Iesco, Gepco and Fesco. The three are considered the most viable Discos among the 11 electricity distribution companies originally carved out of the Water and Power Development Authority (Wapda) in 1998. The divestment is aimed at improving service quality through private-sector management practices. The transaction offers investors an opportunity to acquire between 51pc and 100pc shareholding, along with management control, in each of the three distribution companies. The Privatisation Commission set July 7 for submission of expressions of interest (EoIs) for Fesco, August 24 for Gepco and Sept 7 for Iesco. In June, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Privatisation Muhammad Ali told Dawn the first Discos in the country would be sold in 2026-27. “We will run these three parallel transactions and hold bidding one after the other in October, November and December 2026,” he said, adding the transaction structures would have to be “corrected” before October and “we will do it”. He said the Privatisation Commission had completed domestic soft marketing of three Discos of Faisalabad, Gujranwala and Islamabad in seven major cities, with chambers of commerce and industry and business houses and would now be expanding abroad mainly to Saudi Arabia, China and Turkiye and approaching other Middle Eastern capitals — Qatar, Bahrain, Oman and so on — virtually and through transaction advisers to tap in investors and technical operators. The uniform consumer tariff will continue for the time being, but privatisation, resulting efficiency gains, and the absorption of surplus capacity would reduce the average uniform tariff, he hoped. He said there was robust investor interest in the power sector. However, they wanted an 18pc dollar-based return, an end to uniform consumer tariffs, permission for self-power generation by new owners, freedom for the private sector to ‘buy and sell electricity’, and the government’s exit from the sector. They also wanted 8-10 year tariff visibility, including investment plans. Ali said the government would not allow dollar-based returns at all. “We will provide rupee-based returns of 14-15pc plus key performance indicators (KPIs) that allow profitability of up to 18-20pc while sharing efficiency gains.” Fesco, Gepco and Iesco collectively serve more than 14 million consumers across major industrial, commercial and urban centres of Punjab, the Islamabad region, and parts of Azad Jammu and Kashmir. Their privatisation forms part of the government’s broader economic reform agenda aimed at improving efficiency, strengthening service delivery, attracting foreign and domestic investment, and promoting sustainable growth in Pakistan’s power sector, the Privatisation Commission has said. Alongside these three transactions, the PM’s adviser had said that the Sukkur and Hyderabad electric companies would also be restructured and improved to complete their privatisation by August-September next year.

‘No sovereignty over East Jerusalem’: Dar condemns Al-Aqsa incursions by ‘extremist Israeli settlers’. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Wednesday said that Israel has no sovereignty over East Jerusalem and its holy sites, condemning the incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque by “extremist Israeli settlers”. Addressing the ministerial conference in Amman, Jordan, he said that the illegal actions of Israel — the occupying power in occupied Palestine — continued to threaten the sanctity and historical character of the holy sites in Jerusalem. “They undermine international law, disregard UN resolutions, and further erode the prospect of a just, comprehensive and lasting peace.” “Pakistan condemns in the strongest possible terms the continued incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque by extremist Israeli settlers encouraged by senior Israeli ministers and carried out under the protection of occupying forces,” FM Dar stated. By deliberately undermining the religious and historical status of Jerusalem, FM Dar emphasised that Israel was provoking the sentiments of billions of Muslims across the globe. “This appears not only an attempt to undermine regional peace, security and stability but also to drag followers of various religions into a wider conflict,” he said, adding, “We cannot and must not allow that.” “Pakistan condemns Israeli actions and provocations in the strongest possible terms,” he said. He stressed that there should be no ambiguity that Israel has no sovereignty over occupied East Jerusalem and its Islamic and Christian holy sites. “All measures seeking to alter its character and status are null and void and without any legal effect,” he added. The foreign minister said Pakistan reaffirmed its support for the historic and special role played by Jordan and recognised the Jerusalem Endowment and Al-Aqsa Affairs Department, affiliated with the Jordanian Ministry of Awqaf and Islamic Affairs, as the legal authority with exclusive jurisdiction over the administration of Al-Aqsa Mosque. Moreover, FM Dar said that Pakistan also remained “deeply concerned” over the continuous expansion of illegal Israeli settlements, the establishment of new settlements and the continued oppression of the Palestinian people. “These policies violate international law and further entrench an unlawful occupation.” In Gaza, he said that the humanitarian situation was extremely fragile. “The ceasefire and the implementation of the elements of the Gaza Peace Plan have yielded some improvements; however, 59pc of the population still faces food insecurity and health crises,” FM Dar said. Since the ceasefire, he said that over 1,100 Palestinians had been killed, which called into question the full and faithful implementation of the Gaza Peace Plan. “Arab and Islamic countries must act with unity, resolve and collective action and should first reaffirm the protection of Jerusalem and the holy sites, demanding an immediate cessation of all violations against Al-Aqsa Mosque, preservation of the historical and legal status quo, and unrestricted access to the Old City of Jerusalem and the holy sites,” he said. He said that Arab and Islamic countries should also reject “illegal Israeli settlement activities, annexation attempts, forced displacements, and demographic changes in the occupied Palestinian territory”. “We should support the full and faithful implementation of the comprehensive plan to end the Gaza conflict and UNSC Resolution No. 2803,” the foreign minister said, adding, “We should also strengthen Arab and Islamic coordination and diplomatic efforts to ensure the protection of the Kashmiri people.” Meetings on sidelines FM Dar also held one-on-one meetings with the foreign ministers of Turkiye, Algeria and Egypt on the sidelines of the ministerial meeting on Jerusalem, the FO said. In his meeting with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, FM Dar “exchanged views on regional and international issues of mutual interest,” it said. During his meeting with Egyptian Foreign Minister Dr Badr Abdelatty, Dar discussed Pakistan-Egypt relations, regional and international developments, and exchanged views on matters of mutual interest, the FO said. Meanwhile, in his meeting with Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmad Attaf, FM Dar “discussed Pakistan-Algeria bilateral relations and explored ways to enhance cooperation in trade, investment, information technology, agriculture and other areas of mutual interest”. Moreover, the foreign ministers of the R-4 Group, comprising Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, also met in Amman on the sidelines of the ministerial meeting on Jerusalem, the FO said. “The ministers reiterated their unwavering support for the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people, including their right to self-determination and the establishment of an independent, sovereign Palestinian state on the basis of the June 4, 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital, in accordance with relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions,” it added. According to the FO, the R-4 Group’s foreign ministers reaffirmed that a “just, comprehensive and lasting settlement” of the Palestinian issue remained indispensable to achieving enduring peace and stability in the Middle East. The ministers also reviewed the evolving regional situation and reaffirmed the importance of continued consultation and close coordination among the four countries in advancing regional stability, emphasising that dialogue and diplomacy remained essential to fostering stability and preventing further escalation in the region, the FO stated. DPM meets Jordanian counterpart Dar met his Jordanian counterpart, with the “deteriorating situation in the occupied West Bank” coming under discussion, according to the Foreign Office (FO). The FO said Dar met Jordan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates Ayman Safadi on the sidelines of a Ministerial Meeting in Amman to discuss the situation in occupied Jerusalem. The FO said that the foreign ministers exchanged views on regional developments, in particular on the deteriorating situation in the occupied West Bank. Dar appreciated Jordan’s role in safeguarding the Islamic and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem and its support for the Palestinian people, it added. “The two leaders welcomed the growing momentum in Pakistan–Jordan bilateral relations and reaffirmed [their commitment] to further enhancing cooperation across political, defence, economic, educational, cultural and people-to-people domains,” it added. Dar and Safadi also discussed the situation in the region, including the recent developments in the conflict between the United States and Iran. They underscored the importance of dialogue and diplomacy for de-escalation and reaffirmed their close coordination at bilateral and multilateral levels to promote peace and stability, including at the United Nations and Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, the statement added. Separately, Dar also held a bilateral meeting with Abdisalam Abdi Ali, the Minister for Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of Somalia. Alongside exchanging views on regional developments, the foreign ministers also reviewed the longstanding fraternal ties between the two countries. According to the FO, they discussed ways to further strengthen cooperation in the “political, economic, defence, education, and capacity-building sectors”. They also reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining close coordination at multilateral forums, it added. According to the FO, Dar is in Jordan to attend a ministerial meeting aimed at formulating a unified position on the situation in occupied Jerusalem. It said that he would “reaffirm Pakistan’s unwavering support for the Palestinian people and their just cause” at the ministerial meeting bringing together foreign ministers from Arab League member states and a group of Islamic countries to discuss the deteriorating situation in occupied Jerusalem. The foreign minister is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts on the sidelines of the meeting to exchange views on regional developments including Palestine. The FO termed Dar’s participation in the ministerial meeting “a manifestation of Pakistan’s principled support for the Palestinian people” and its commitment to the establishment of an “independent, sovereign and contiguous” State of Palestine based on pre-1967 borders, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital. Pakistan and other Muslim countries have repeatedly condemned “continued incursions by extremist Israeli settlers” into Al Aqsa Mosque — Islam’s third-holiest site, located in east Jerusalem, which Israel captured in 1967 and later annexed. The Al-Aqsa compound is a central symbol of Palestinian identity and also a frequent flashpoint. Under long-standing arrangements, Jewish people may visit the compound, but are not permitted to pray there. While Israel says it is committed to maintaining this status quo, Palestinians fear it is being eroded. The foreign ministers of Pakistan and eight other Muslim countries in June expressed their “categorical rejection” of any attempts to alter the historical and legal status quo in Jerusalem and its Islamic and Christian holy sites.

India panel warns Meta over Modi video removal. An Indian parliamentary panel called on Wednesday for Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg to apologise for the temporary removal of a video of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. India, the world’s most populous country, is Meta’s largest market by users, with hundreds of millions of people using Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. Modi’s video, addressing students during youth-led protests on July 23, was briefly removed from Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram, but was later restored. Meta has said it was caused by technical error. Nishikant Dubey, who heads the parliamentary committee on communications and information technology, said the panel blamed Meta. “Deleting the prime minister’s video was not the work of an intermediary, but that of a publisher,” Dubey said, a lawmaker in Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). “Zuckerberg will have to apologise within three days.” Joel Kaplan, chief global affairs officer at Meta, said he met with India’s Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on Wednesday and apologised. “I apologised to the minister on behalf of Meta for the error restricting PM Modi’s post,” Kaplan said in a statement. India’s parliamentary standing committees scrutinise government policies and can summon officials and company executives to answer questions. However, they cannot themselves impose penalties, revoke legal protections or direct prosecutions. Any action against an online platform would have to be taken by the government or the courts under existing law. Dubey said that the committee had written to the interior and technology ministries demanding action. “If he does not apologise, then all the safe harbour protections that have been provided to his social media platforms should end,” Dubey told reporters. Modi posted the vertical video, speaking directly to the camera, on July 23 — during the height of protests led by the online Cockroach Janta Party movement. The demonstrations, which began in New Delhi, were sparked by anger over exam irregularities but grew into a wider movement over jobs, youth opportunities and what critics describe as Modi’s increasingly authoritarian rule . Modi, a keen user of X, turned to Instagram — issuing his first vertical videos to tap into the youth medium of choice. In the video, Modi assured students that the government would implement stricter laws and harsher punishments against paper leaks. Zuckerberg apologises to India government over Meta content and errors, local media says Zuckerberg has apologised to the Indian government over child sexual abuse material on the company’s platforms and for operational errors, local television channels reported on Wednesday. Zuckerberg apologised for the presence of the material, as well as deepfake content and operational lapses on Meta’s platforms, financial news publication Moneycontrol reported, citing sources. The publication added the apology was conveyed during a meeting between Meta executives and Indian government officials on Tuesday. Meta, whose major social media apps include Facebook and Instagram, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Roads blocked, traffic disrupted as PTI holds rally near Karachi Press Club. KARACHI: The PTI held a protest near the Karachi Press Club (KPC) on Wednesday to mark three years since the imprisonment of party founder Imran Khan and demand his release. The demonstration led to traffic disruptions in the surrounding areas after authorities blocked routes leading to the venue, causing severe congestion and leaving commuters stranded for extended periods. A screenshot showing closed roads in Karachi’s Saddar Town area. — Screengrab from Google Maps A police official, who wished not to be named, said that some PTI workers and leaders were detained near the Press Club. They confirmed that police resorted to tear gas shelling and used baton charges to disperse the demonstrators, adding that after the police action, the road was cleared for traffic in the evening. The PTI in a statement said it staged demonstrations in Karachi, Hyderabad, Mirpurkhas, Nawabshah, Umerkot, Mithi and other parts of Sindh, with participants demanding Imran’s release. In Karachi, the demonstration was led by PTI Sindh President Haleem Adil Sheikh, Karachi President Raja Azhar, PTI Sindh General Secretary Dr Masroor Sial and Karachi General Secretary Arsalan Khalid. They and other party leaders led workers towards the Karachi Press Club, according to the statement. “However, according to the party, police blocked all routes leading to the Press Club by placing containers and completely sealed the area to stop protesters from reaching the venue,” the statement claimed. “PTI workers later held a peaceful demonstration near Zaibunnisa Street and Fawara Chowk in Saddar. The party alleged that police resorted to tear gas shelling and baton charge against peaceful protesters, leaving several workers injured,” it alleged. PTI demonstrators stage a protest in Karachi’s Saddar Town area on August 5, 2026. — Photo courtesy PTI The PTI alleged that the police arrested more than ten workers in the metropolis, including Sial. The party further claimed that six PTI workers were arrested in Pano Aqil and fifteen workers in Kandhkot, with cases also registered against them. Addressing the protesters, Sheikh demanded the immediate release of Dr Masroor Sial and all detained workers in Karachi, Pano Aqil and Kandhkot, while Raza Azhar said the PTI “formally submitted an application seeking permission for the peaceful protest, yet police still resorted to unlawful use of force”. Sheikh also took to X and claimed that the route to the KPC had been blocked by containers, slamming the PPP government for sealing off the area. “The Karachi Press Club is neither a Red Zone nor a sensitive security area, yet the PPP government has blocked public access and trampled the constitutional right to peaceful assembly,” he wrote. Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah took notice of the congestion and issued strict instructions to the Sindh inspector general and the Karachi additional inspector general to restore traffic flow. “Traffic should be cleared from Sadar, Old City Area, MA Jinnah Road and Zainab Market immediately,” he was quoted as saying in a statement from his office. “Additional traffic police personnel should be deployed on the roads and a report should be submitted.” He further ordered that queues of cars on Napier Road, Regal Chowk and Bolton Market should also be cleared. Similarly, Sindh Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar sought details from the Karachi Traffic deputy inspector general (DIG) on the traffic jams in the city, with a statement from his office saying that the cause behind the disruption should be determined. “District police should help traffic police in clearing the roads and highways,” Lanjar was quoted as saying. “The difficulties faced by citizens should be immediately addressed.” He ordered that traffic police personnel should be stationed on all major arteries and pressure points to manage the flow of traffic, adding that they need to be cleared immediately to restore traffic flow. “In case of traffic flow being affected, alternative routes should be arranged immediately,” Lanjar added. “Citizens should face minimum difficulties; traffic flow should be ensured at all costs.” Islamabad In Islamabad, the party staged a protest on Karnal Sher Khan Shaheed Road, formerly known as IJP Road, to mark three years since Imran’s imprisonment. The rally was led by PTI Islamabad Regional President Amir Mughal and Regional General Secretary Malik Amir Ali Awan. Mughal told Dawn that it had been decided that only one protest would take place in the federal capital, with Karnal Sher Khan Shaheed Road selected for “a show of power”. Participants chanted slogans and displayed placards highlighting issues including Imran’s imprisonment, the situation in Indian-occupied Kashmir, inflation, unemployment, law and order, and other matters. Hyderabad Similarly, the PTI staged a rally in Hyderabad, but it remained peaceful and no arrests were made by police as witnessed elsewhere. The rally was staged on the joint call of PTI and Tehreek Tahfuz Aayeen-e-Pakistan (TTAP) to mark three years of Imran’s imprisonment, starting from Liberty Chowk and culminating outside the local press club. PTI Hyderabad President Mohsin Ghumman, PTI Sindh Deputy General Secretary Arif Ghafoor Sheikh and others attended. The rally remained peaceful, but according to Mohsin Ghumman, police did not allow the demonstrators to set up camps. Police, however, didn’t make any arrests, he confirmed. Activists and workers gathered at Hyder Chowk before reaching the local press club, where they staged a sit-in and played party songs and a recorded clip of Imran’s past speech, amid vociferous slogans. Addressing protesters outside the press club, PTI leaders paid tributes to party workers for their steadfastness. Imran — imprisoned since Aug 5, 2023, for concealing details of Toshakhana gifts — is serving a 14-year sentence at Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail in a £190 million corruption case, also known as the Al-Qadir Trust case . While imprisoned, Imran has not met his family or party leaders since his sister Uzma Khanum met him last December, despite a court order from the Islamabad High Court mandating meetings on Tuesdays and Thursdays. His sisters have staged regular sit-ins on Tuesdays, demanding meetings with the ex-premier and that he be treated for a severe eye condition. His eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) — came to light in late January and he receives government-provided treatment . The government and the opposition have been engaged in a blame game , with the latter accusing the former of a lack of transparency in not ensuring appropriate treatment for Imran, and not allowing his personal physicians access to him. The government denies these allegations. The opposition has also demanded that the former premier be shifted to Shifa International Hospital, be treated in the presence of his personal physicians and allowed to meet his family.

Pakistan, Iran agree to keep border crossings open round the clock to boost trade. Pakistan and Iran on Wednesday agreed to further expand trade ties by keeping border crossings open round the clock, improving logistics and harmonising customs procedures. The development came during a meeting between Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and a six-member Iranian delegation, led by Iran’s Minister for Industry, Mine and Trade Mohammad Atabak, in Islamabad, according to a statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). During the meeting, the prime minister said that Pakistan highly valued its relations with its close, brotherly neighbour Iran, the PMO said. “Pakistan will continue its sincere efforts for peace in the region,” PM Shehbaz was quoted as saying. He added that he had recently held a productive discussion with Iranian President Dr Masoud Pezeshkian on establishing lasting peace in the region and further enhancing Pakistan-Iran bilateral relations, particularly in trade, the statement said. During the meeting, the prime minister expressed hope that sustained efforts would enable both countries to achieve the bilateral trade target of $10 billion set by their leadership, it added. “Both countries will benefit from increased trade, particularly in food, agricultural commodities and related products,” PM Shehbaz said. According to the statement, the meeting also agreed to promote border trade between Pakistan and Iran by expanding facilities to keep border crossings open 24 hours a day. “Both sides also agreed to enhance cooperation in the mining sector, particularly in the processing and value addition of precious stones,” it stated. The Iranian minister said he was grateful to Pakistan for the warm welcome and excellent hospitality. He praised the Pakistani leadership and people for their “sincere diplomatic efforts for regional peace and their expression of solidarity with Iran,” the statement said. “Iran is keen to further expand its economic and trade relations with Pakistan,” Atabak was quoted as saying. “Technical-level negotiations on a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) between Pakistan and Iran are currently underway,” he added. On Tuesday, both countries also reiterated their resolve to expand bilateral trade to $10 billion. In April, Pakistan’s commerce ministry had notified six transit routes for the transportation of goods to Iran via Pakistani sea ports in Gwadar and Karachi. The development had come amid reports that thousands of containers destined for Iran are awaiting clearance at Pakistani ports. Since March this year, both countries have rolled out a series of measures to facilitate border trade, including easing customs procedures, formalising Taftan as a customs station, and notifying new transit routes, against the backdrop of the ongoing US-Iran conflict in the Middle East that has strained economies in the region and beyond.

Sindh restores five-day working week for schools, colleges.
